items.stem: A furniture maker pays for timber on delivery, takes 30 days to make and sell its products and gives customers 60 days' credit. Calculate the length of its working capital cycle and suggest one way to shorten it.
items.answer: About 90 days (0 days' credit from suppliers + 30 days production/storage + 60 days customer credit). Shorten by negotiating credit with timber suppliers, reducing customer credit or offering early-payment discounts.
items.markingKey: About 90 days (0 days' credit from suppliers + 30 days production/storage + 60 days customer credit). Shorten by negotiating credit with timber suppliers, reducing customer credit or offering early-payment discounts.

items.stem: In its first month NordBike Ltd made sales of €150,000, of which 75% were on 60-day credit. Its costs for the month were €112,500, of which it paid 70% in cash during the month. Calculate the profit for the month and the net cash flow, and explain why they differ.
items.answer: Profit = €150,000 − €112,500 = €37,500. Cash in = €37,500; cash out = €78,750; net cash flow = −€41,250. They differ because credit sales count as revenue before the cash is received, unpaid costs are not yet cash outflows.

items.stem: Project A costs $60,000 and returns $20,000 a year for 5 years. Project B costs $60,000 and returns $30,000 in year 1, $20,000 in year 2 and $10,000 a year for years 3-5. Calculate the payback period of each and explain which a cash-strapped firm should prefer.
items.answer: Payback A: 20,000 × 3 = 60,000, so 3 years. Payback B: 30,000 + 20,000 = 50,000 after 2 years; the remaining 10,000 comes from year 3, so 3 years. The paybacks are equal, so compare ARR: A = ((100,000 − 60,000) / 5) / 60,000 × 100 = 13.3%; B = ((80,000 − 60,000) / 5) / 60,000 × 100 = 6.7%. A cash-strapped firm gets the same payback from both but A is more profitable, so it should choose A (B does return more cash earlier, in year 1).
